title: Cotangent coefficient bases and functorial linearization of formal algebra maps
statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $m,n\ge0$, $S=F[[t_1,\ldots,t_m]]$, $T=F[[z_1,\ldots,z_n]]$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series], and $\mathfrak a=(t_1,\ldots,t_m)$, $\mathfrak b=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$. Regard the quotients $\mathfrak a/\mathfrak a^2$ and $\mathfrak b/\mathfrak b^2$ as $F$-vector spaces; a class means the class of an element of the indicated ideal modulo its square. Their coefficient maps $[h]\mapsto([t_i]h)_i$ and $[g]\mapsto([z_j]g)_j$ are $F$-linear isomorphisms to $F^m$ and $F^n$, sending the variable classes to the standard bases. Here $[t_i]h$ and $[z_j]g$ denote the respective linear coefficients. Let $\psi:S\to T$ be an $F$-algebra homomorphism satisfying $\psi(\mathfrak a)\subseteq\mathfrak b$. It preserves constant coefficients and induces an $F$-linear map $\bar\psi:\mathfrak a/\mathfrak a^2\to\mathfrak b/\mathfrak b^2$. Define the $m\times n$ matrix $L_\psi$ [def-weil-matrix] by $(L_\psi)_{ij}=[z_j]\psi(t_i)$. In the coefficient bases this map sends a coefficient row $v$ to $vL_\psi$; equivalently, for every $h\in\mathfrak a$,
$$[z_j]\psi(h)=\sum_{i=1}^m([t_i]h)(L_\psi)_{ij}.$$
For every $r\ge0$, $U=F[[w_1,\ldots,w_r]]$, $\mathfrak c=(w_1,\ldots,w_r)$ and $F$-algebra homomorphism $\theta:T\to U$ with $\theta(\mathfrak b)\subseteq\mathfrak c$, the induced quotient maps compose and
$$L_{\theta\circ\psi}=L_\psi L_\theta,\qquad L_{\mathrm{id}_S}=I_m.$$
All statements include zero variables, zero-dimensional quotients and the corresponding empty matrices.

proof.text: Write $c(f)$ for the constant coefficient and $\ell_i(f)$ for the coefficient of the $i$th variable. The Cauchy product in [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series] gives $c(fg)=c(f)c(g)$ and $\ell_i(fg)=c(f)\ell_i(g)+\ell_i(f)c(g)$: the only decompositions of the exponent $e_i$ are $(0,e_i)$ and $(e_i,0)$. Coefficients are additive and $F$-linear. Work first in $S$, with variable ideal $\mathfrak a$. Every element of $\mathfrak a$ is a finite sum of multiples of the $t_i$, hence has zero constant coefficient. The displayed formula shows that products of two such elements have zero linear coefficients as well. Since an element of $\mathfrak a^2$ is a finite sum of these products, both its constant and all its linear coefficients vanish. The identical argument applies in $T$ and $U$.

source.place: Tag 0C4B (lemma-fitting-ideal-well-defined), final coordinate-change paragraph; agent-supplied details of the cotangent linearization implicit in the invertible-Jacobian assertion.

proof.text: For any $h\in S$, set $q=h-c(h)-\sum_i\ell_i(h)t_i$, viewing scalars as constant series. Direct coefficient extraction gives $c(q)=0$ and $\ell_i(q)=0$ for every $i$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-quadratic-ideal] to obtain $q\in\mathfrak a^2$. In particular, $c(h)=0$ implies $h\in\mathfrak a$, and therefore $\mathfrak a=\ker c$. For $h\in\mathfrak a$, the resulting identity $[h]=\sum_i\ell_i(h)[t_i]$ proves that the coefficient map on $\mathfrak a/\mathfrak a^2$ has inverse $v\mapsto[\sum_i v_it_i]$. Step 1 ensures it is well-defined, and direct extraction of coefficients proves that the two maps are inverse and $F$-linear and take variable classes to the standard basis. Repeat with the finite variable sets for $T$ and $U$.

proof.text: For any $h\in S$, Step 2 gives $h-c(h)\in\mathfrak a$. Its image lies in $\mathfrak b$, whose elements have zero constant coefficient by Step 1. Since $\psi$ fixes $F$, this gives $c(\psi(h))=c(h)$. Moreover $\psi(\mathfrak a^2)\subseteq\mathfrak b^2$: write an element as a finite sum $\sum_k a_ka'_k$ with $a_k,a'_k\in\mathfrak a$ and apply multiplicativity and additivity. Thus $[h]\mapsto[\psi(h)]$ is independent of the representative and is an $F$-linear map, because $\psi$ is additive and fixes scalar multiplication. This constructs the asserted $\bar\psi$. The same argument constructs $\bar\theta$ and the quotient map of $\theta\circ\psi$.

source.place: Tag 0C4B (lemma-fitting-ideal-well-defined), final coordinate-change paragraph; agent-supplied details of the cotangent linearization implicit in the invertible-Jacobian assertion.

proof.text: For $h\in\mathfrak a$, the remainder formula of Step 2 reads $h=\sum_i\ell_i(h)t_i+q$ with $q\in\mathfrak a^2$. Applying $\psi$ gives $\psi(h)=\sum_i\ell_i(h)\psi(t_i)+\psi(q)$, where $\psi(q)\in\mathfrak b^2$ by Step 3. Step 1 says its linear coefficients vanish. Taking the $z_j$ coefficient therefore gives $[z_j]\psi(h)=\sum_i\ell_i(h)[z_j]\psi(t_i)=\sum_i\ell_i(h)(L_\psi)_{ij}$. By the coefficient isomorphisms of Step 2 this is exactly the row formula $v\mapsto vL_\psi$.

source.place: Tag 0C4B (lemma-fitting-ideal-well-defined), final coordinate-change paragraph; agent-supplied details of the cotangent linearization implicit in the invertible-Jacobian assertion.

proof.text: On a representative $h\in\mathfrak a$, both $\overline{\theta\circ\psi}([h])$ and $(\bar\theta\circ\bar\psi)([h])$ are $[\theta(\psi(h))]$, so the quotient maps compose. Apply Step 4 to $\theta$ and the element $\psi(t_i)\in\mathfrak b$: for every $i,k$, $[w_k]\theta(\psi(t_i))=\sum_j([z_j]\psi(t_i))([w_k]\theta(z_j))=\sum_j(L_\psi)_{ij}(L_\theta)_{jk}$. By the definition of matrix multiplication this gives $L_{\theta\circ\psi}=L_\psi L_\theta$. Finally $[t_j]t_i=\delta_{ij}$ gives $L_{\mathrm{id}_S}=I_m$. If any variable set is empty, its ideal and cotangent quotient are zero, all corresponding sums are empty, and the same formulas give the unique maps and the appropriate empty matrices. No continuity of $\psi$ or $\theta$ has been used.
